analysis.one_liner: Makes oil spillers pay cleanup and damage costs, with a federal fund and new spill-prevention rules for tankers.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill 99-0 on August 4, 1989, and on November 19 folded it into a House companion, H.R. 1465, which Congress passed and which became the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: Passed months after the Exxon Valdez spill, this bill would make vessel and facility owners strictly liable for oil spill cleanup costs and for damages to property, natural resources, and people's lost income — including fishermen, subsistence users, and coastal businesses. It creates an Oil Spill Compensation Fund that pays claims when the spiller is unknown, insolvent, or beyond its liability cap, up to $1 billion per incident, and adds prevention rules: approved spill response plans with practice drills, regional response teams, extra officers on tanker bridges, alcohol testing for tanker crews, and special safeguards at Valdez and Bligh Reef. The Senate passed it unanimously, then folded it into the House companion H.R. 1465, which carried these provisions to enactment as the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, commercial and subsistence fishermen, and coastal businesses gain a guaranteed path to compensation: polluters must pay removal costs and damages for lost property, lost use of natural resources (including subsistence use), and lost income or profits, and the federal fund pays when the responsible party cannot. State governments gain power to respond immediately and to keep stricter state rules on the books. Taxpayers gain because the burden of cleanup shifts from the public to the oil industry, and the public gains natural-resource trustees who recover money specifically for restoration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fishermen, coastal communities, states, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Makes oil spillers strictly liable for all removal costs and for damages including destroyed property, loss of subsistence use of natural resources, and lost income, profits, or earning capacity — without regard to who owns the damaged property or resources.

Creates an Oil Spill Compensation Fund that pays removal costs and damage claims when the spiller is unknown, unidentifiable, or fails to pay, up to $1 billion per incident, and lets governors obligate $250,000 per discharge for immediate state response.

Preserves and even strengthens state authority: nothing in the bill preempts states from imposing additional liability, keeping their own oil spill funds, or enforcing financial responsibility requirements.

Requires prevention, not just payment: owners must file and follow approved contingency plans capable of handling a worst-case discharge, submit to inspections and surprise drills twice a year, and face civil penalties for noncompliance.

Directs regional oil spill response teams (funded up to $50 million from the fund) to be stationed for every coastal region and inland waters, capable of responding to a worst-case spill, with preference in cleanup contracts for local businesses in the affected area.

Targets the exact failure that caused the Exxon Valdez disaster: extra deck officers and lookouts on tanker bridges, two licensed pilots, position checks every six minutes, random alcohol testing of safety-sensitive crew, state-licensed pilots at Valdez, a navigational light at Bligh Reef, and expanded vessel tracking in Prince William Sound.
Makes federal and state officials trustees who recover natural resource damages from spillers, with the money used only to restore, replace, or acquire the equivalent of the injured resources.

Raises the stakes for polluters: civil penalties of up to $25,000 per day or $1,000 per barrel, longer prison terms for knowing discharges and for failing to report spills, and treble punitive damages for those who refuse ordered cleanup.

analysis.who_pays: Vessel owners, tanker operators, and onshore/offshore oil facility owners pay through strict liability, mandatory financial responsibility (insurance, bonds, or letters of credit large enough to cover their maximum liability), contingency plans, inspections, drills, and user fees for plan review and inspections. Oil companies also lose their old dedicated liability funds, which are folded into the new fund. A share of the cost is passed through to anyone who buys oil: the fund is financed through the per-barrel oil tax under the Internal Revenue Code and through Treasury advances that must be repaid with interest, so catastrophic spills beyond the caps ultimately come back to oil purchasers and taxpayers. Shipping costs from the new crewing, equipment, and insurance requirements also flow into oil prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil shippers and facility owners; oil buyers via fund taxes

drawbacks.text: Liability is capped: tankers at $1,000 per gross ton or $10 million (whichever is greater), other vessels at $600 per gross ton or $500,000, and facilities at $350 million — far below what a catastrophe like the Exxon Valdez spill, which Congress noted would cost millions to clean up, actually costs. Damages above the cap fall to the federal fund, which itself is capped at $1 billion per incident, so victims and taxpayers can be left holding the rest of a truly catastrophic spill's costs.

The double-hull requirement is discretionary, not mandatory: the bill directs the Secretary to require double hulls and bottoms on affected oil tankers unless he determines the requirement would not enhance navigation safety — a built-in escape hatch the shipping industry could use.

Response readiness depends heavily on the industry itself: cleanup capability rests on company-written contingency plans, private contractors, and industry oil spill response organizations, so if companies understate their worst case or plans are approved loosely, the promised readiness may not materialize. The fund also caps its oil spill research spending at $25 million a year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a good one for ordinary people: instead of communities and taxpayers absorbing spill damage, the companies that move and store oil must insure against their full liability, plan for worst-case spills, and pay into a fund that guarantees compensation. The honest weaknesses are the liability caps and the $1 billion per-incident fund ceiling, which cap the industry's downside well below the cost of a worst-case disaster and quietly shift the tail risk back to oil purchasers and taxpayers; the discretionary double-hull provision is another concession. Still, this replaced a patchwork of far weaker funds with strict liability, state powers preserved, and real prevention mandates — a substantial net gain for coastal residents, fishermen, and the public.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it unanimously, the House never voted on the bill itself, and the Senate instead folded it into a House companion, H.R. 1465, which carried the provisions to enactment as the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.

narrative.text: Senator George Mitchell introduced the bill on April 4, 1989, weeks after the Exxon Valdez ran aground in Prince William Sound, spilling eleven million gallons of crude oil — the largest oil spill in U.S. history — with the bill's findings citing damage to Alaska's commercial fishery and to Native villages and subsistence users.

The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee held hearings in July 1989, ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments on July 27, and reported it to the Senate on July 28 with a written report and additional views.
The Senate took it up by unanimous consent on August 3 and passed it with amendments on August 4 by a vote of 99-0 — all 55 Democrats and 44 of 45 Republicans in favor.

The House received the bill on September 6 but held it at the desk and never voted on it; on November 19 the Senate incorporated the measure into H.R. 1465 and passed that companion bill in lieu of S. 686 by voice vote.

That vehicle, H.R. 1465, went on to enactment as the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, the law that established the modern polluter-pays and Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund regime — so the substance of S. 686 became law even though the bill itself never cleared the House under its own number.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities, fishermen, and taxpayers came out ahead: the polluter-pays regime and prevention mandates they needed became law through H.R. 1465. Oil shippers also did comparatively well, since the enacted framework carried liability caps and a $1 billion-per-incident fund ceiling that limit their exposure in a true catastrophe.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal communities, fishermen, and taxpayers; shippers kept caps

for.name: Sen. George J. Mitchell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 4, 1989 and steered it through committee to a 99-0 Senate passage four months after the Exxon Valdez spill.

for.name: Sen. Quentin Burdick
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: His committee held hearings, ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments, and reported it to the Senate with Report 101-94 on July 28, 1989.

for.name: 55 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final Senate passage.

for.name: 44 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final Senate passage.

for.name: 15 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing before it reached the floor.

against.name: Oil shipping and marine insurance interests
against.role: Tanker owners, oil transporters, and their insurers
against.what_they_did: Pressed during the 1989-90 debate to cap spill liability rather than face unlimited exposure; the Senate bill reflects that in caps of $1,000 per gross ton or $10 million for tankers, $350 million for facilities, and a $1 billion per-incident cap on the compensation fund.

against.name: House leadership (no floor action on S. 686)
against.what_they_did: Held the Senate-passed bill at the desk for over two months and never brought it to a vote; the Senate instead moved the substance to H.R. 1465.

sides.party_line_note: Final Senate passage was 99-0 — every voting Democrat (55) and all but one voting Republican (44 of 45) voted yes, with no opposition in the record.

industries.note: They gain enforceable liability caps ($1,000 per gross ton or $10 million for tankers) and a federal fund that absorbs claims above their cap, but lose through strict liability, mandatory financial responsibility, contingency plans, extra bridge crews, alcohol testing, and potential double-hull requirements. Their interest in capping liability runs against full compensation for spill victims, since catastrophic costs above the caps shift to the fund and oil purchasers.

industries.industry: Oil producers and terminal operators (including the Alyeska pipeline)
industries.note: Facility liability is capped at $350 million and old dedicated funds (Trans-Alaska Pipeline Liability Fund, Offshore Oil Pollution Compensation Fund) are folded into the new fund, but their facilities face contingency planning, inspection, a $100 million financial responsibility floor for offshore facilities, and Title V environmental oversight and monitoring programs at the Valdez and Kenai terminals with advisory councils and citizen monitoring.

Financial responsibility requirements force vessel and facility owners to buy insurance, surety bonds, guarantees, or letters of credit sized to their maximum liability, creating a large mandated market — though claims can be brought directly against guarantors up to the policy amount.

industries.industry: Oil spill response and cleanup contractors
industries.note: Regional response teams must arrange with private contractors, companies must pre-position equipment and run drills, and the fund bankrolls team setup (up to $50 million) and reimburses removal participants, with preference for local businesses in affected areas.

These diffuse industries gain directly: the bill makes spillers liable for lost income, profits, and earning capacity from damaged resources, without regard to ownership, and funds restoration of the fisheries and wildlife they depend on.
